newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat says world forum aims to rescue peace.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says world forum aims to rescue peace.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting of U.S., European and Arab envoys would save Middle East peace from a crisis over Israeli settlement plans in the West Bank.
Asked why he had called the meeting for Saturday in the self-ruled Gaza Strip, Arafat told reporters: "To protect the peace process."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in Russia on a trip overshadowed by growing world criticism, told a Moscow news conference he was "fed up" with charges Israel was violating peace deals with the Palestinians.

The United States, Israel's closest ally, tightened the noose of international pressure around the Jewish state on Wednesday by saying it would send Edward Abington, the consul general in Jerusalem, to the Gaza meeting.

"We regard this as a briefing on Arafat's concerns about the peace process," said Ambassador Martin Indyk in defence of U.S. participation despite the objections raised by Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy when they met on Wednesday.

Netanyahu, elected last year on a vow to get tough in peace talks, has enraged Palestinians by deciding to build a new Jewish settlement and to limit the first of three Israeli troop pullbacks in the West Bank to a third of what they wanted.

Palestinians accuse him of trying to circumvent them as his peace partners and of violating Israeli-PLO peace accords by planning to build the settlement on land in Arab East Jerusalem they say is due to be the subject of future negotiation.
"Does Israel really think that the world approves and would stay silent? Israel will realise sooner or later that it is wrong and the world is right," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
He said Arafat would open the Gaza meeting on Saturday with a speech at 1100 (0900 GMT). Participants would be invited to speak and Palestinians would present a "working paper".
At the United Nations on Wednesday, the General Assembly planned a debate expected to end in overwhelming support for a demand that Israel abandon its plans to build 6,500 houses at the site.
In a letter this week to Netanyahu, King Hussein, the Israeli leader's closest Arab peace partner, warned the lives of Arabs and Jews were sliding towards an "abyss of bloodshed".

"I'm getting, frankly, fed up with the idea that everything we do is a violation of the (peace) agreement, and everything the Palestinians say is in compliance with the agreement," Netanyahu told reporters in Moscow.
Israel's Ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben-Elissar, told Israel Radio: "I don't think the government has to change its decisions. We will stick to the decisions and defend them."

Arafat refused to take two telephone calls from Netanyahu on Monday, Israel Television has said. A PLO official said Arafat had refused more than twice since Friday to receive Netanyahu's representatives.
"He doesn't want to talk. We won't force him," Netanyahu said. "I think there's an attempt to create a crisis."
After speaking to reporters, Arafat met a group of 140 Israelis described by an organiser as businessmen whose visit aimed to confirm the importance of contacts and cooperation for the sake of peace.
